Hook: In 1980 the economist Julian Simon offered anyone a bet. Pick any raw materials you like; if their prices, after inflation, are higher in ten years' time, I pay; if lower, you pay. The biologist Paul Ehrlich, who had warned that a growing population would run the world short of food and materials, took it, with two colleagues. Ehrlich chose five metals: chromium, copper, nickel, tin and tungsten. On paper he bought 200 dollars' worth of each, 1,000 dollars in all. On the twenty-ninth of September 1990 the bet was settled. All five metals were cheaper in real terms. In October Ehrlich mailed Simon a cheque for five hundred and seventy-six dollars and seven cents. Behind the bet were two views of scarcity. Ehrlich's: more people and fixed resources, so prices must rise. Simon's: scarcity raises prices, and high prices call forth substitutes, discovery and invention, which push them down again.

Here are three of Ehrlich's metals, the ones the World Bank prices, from its monthly price data, deflated by America's consumer prices. The grey band is the decade of the bet. Copper fell 23 percent in real terms, nickel 14, and tin, whose producers' cartel collapsed in 1985, 77. An equal bundle of the three lost 38 percent. Simon won. But look at the years before 1980 and after 1990: the same prices rose as often as they fell. Chapters one and two ask whether Simon was right, or lucky.

Simon's argument works for metals, because metals have prices. This part is about the things that do not. Its question: what is a tonne of carbon dioxide worth, and what does the answer turn on? Are we running out of things, and what do prices tell us? Why are fish and the air used up, when metals are not? What does warming cost, and how should the future be weighed against the present? And which policies work: taxes, permits, clubs of countries, new technology?
Economics, Built. Part forty-eight: environment and climate.

Here is the plan. Resources that run out and the rule for their prices; the bet, rerun for every decade; and the fishery, a resource that renews itself but is overused anyway. The climate in four equations, fitted to the record of the air and the thermometers, and a climate-economy model built on it. The social cost of carbon, with the discount rate chosen by you, and the problem of fat tails. Taxes, permits, clubs of countries and learning curves; damages measured from the data; and the markets for electricity. Three dials, the people who use these ideas, and the frontier.
Hotelling: In 1931 Harold Hotelling asked what the price of a resource that runs out should do. Think of the owner of an oil field. A barrel sold today earns its price less the cost of getting it out, and the money can be invested at the rate of interest. A barrel left in the ground can be sold next year instead. If owners are to be willing to hold oil in the ground and also to sell some now, the two must be worth the same: the price net of extraction cost, the scarcity rent, must rise at the rate of interest. That is Hotelling's rule. The oil in the ground is an asset, and it must pay like one. And in a competitive market the rent starts at just the level that makes the last barrel come out as the price reaches the point where nobody wants it any more.

Here is the rule at work on an Island mine with two hundred tons of ore, facing a demand that falls to nothing at a price of ten. With an extraction cost of two a ton, the rent starts at 1.01 and grows five percent a year; the price climbs, people buy less and less, and the mine is empty in year 43, just as the price reaches ten. Now let the cost of extraction start higher and fall four percent a year, as better machines and better geology arrive. The rent still rises at the rate of interest, but for 20 years the falling cost wins, and the price falls before it rises: a U. In 1982 Margaret Slade argued that technical progress and ever poorer ores give exactly this U, and found it in the prices of major metals and fuels. The rule says the rent rises. It says nothing about the price, unless you know what happens to cost.

Does the record look like Hotelling? In red, a price that rises five percent a year: since 1960 it would have grown more than twentyfold. The real prices of copper, nickel and tin in 2024 were within about a third of their 1960 levels: copper 1.27 times, nickel 0.97, tin 1.29. Oil, the one most bound up with politics and cartels, rose 4.6 times, mostly in two jumps. Why not twentyfold? Because extraction costs fell, as in the blue path; because new deposits kept being found, so the stock was never fixed; because substitutes arrived, from aluminium for copper to plastic for tin; and because for most metals the scarcity rent is a small part of the price. What does rise, as Hotelling said, is the value of what is truly scarce.
Bet: Suppose the bet had been made in another year. Take the three metals with world prices since 1960, and for every starting year buy equal amounts, then see ten years later whether the bundle is worth more or less after inflation. There are 55 such bets, starting from 1960 to 2014. Red bars are the decades when real prices rose and Ehrlich would have won; green, when they fell and Simon would have. The real bet started in 1980, one of the worst decades for metals: -38 percent. Over all the windows, Ehrlich would have won 28 of 55: about half. A ten-year bet on metal prices is close to a coin toss, decided by booms and busts in demand, not by the slow march of scarcity.

So who was right? Katherine Kiel, Victor Matheson and Kevin Golembiewski reran the bet with Ehrlich's own five metals for every decade from 1900 to 2008. Ehrlich would have won 62 percent of them. Simon's deeper claim survives: over a century the real prices of metals have not climbed the way a scarcity rent would, because human ingenuity kept adding to what could be extracted. But Ehrlich was not foolish to bet: in many decades prices rose, when booms in demand outran supply. And the deeper lesson is about when Simon's mechanism works at all. Metals have owners, and owners have a reason to save what will be worth more later. Fish in the open sea, and the air, have no owners. The rest of this part is about them.
Fishery: Chapter three. Renewable resources: the fishery.

Fish renew themselves, so how can they run out? Scott Gordon answered in 1954. A fish stock grows fastest at middling size. Send out more boats and the catch rises at first, but past a point the stock shrinks so much that the sustained catch falls: the green hill. The red line is what the boats cost. Where anyone may fish, boats keep coming as long as fishing pays, until revenue equals cost and the rent is gone: the sea is fished to where the stock is 0.2 of its natural size. A single owner, or a quota that limits the catch, stops at the effort where the gap between revenue and cost is greatest: half the boats, a stock of 0.6, and a rent worth having. Notice that this is fewer boats even than the effort that catches the most fish. The fish are not lost because they are taken, but because nobody owns the ones left behind.

Over time it is worse than the static picture. Start an Island fishery at its natural size, and let boats enter while fishing pays, as Vernon Smith modelled it in 1969. The fleet grows on yesterday's profits, and by the time catches fall there are far too many boats: in year 8 the stock is down to 3 percent of its natural size, before boats leave and it recovers to 20. Real fisheries have collapsed this way and not come back. Now cap the total catch at 0.1 a year and let the boats trade their shares of it. The stock settles at 72 percent, and the race to fish first is over, because a share is worth more if the stock is kept healthy.

And in the world's oceans? The UN's Food and Agriculture Organization assesses the world's fish stocks. In 1974, 10 percent were overexploited. By 2021, 35.5 percent. Christopher Costello, Steven Gaines and John Lynham studied over 11,000 fisheries and found that catch shares, quotas owned and traded by fishers, halt and even reverse the slide toward collapse: by 2003, the share of quota fisheries that had collapsed was half that of the rest. Property rights did for fish what prices did for metals. The air has no such owner. That is the next chapter.
Climate: Part fifteen met externalities: costs that fall on people who did not choose them. Climate change is the largest there is. Here are the world's emissions of carbon dioxide from fossil fuels and cement since 1850, from the Global Carbon Budget: 39 billion tonnes in 2025. On top, emissions from changing the use of land, mostly from clearing forests. Every tonne mixes into the whole atmosphere within a year or two, and a good part of it stays for centuries. So every tonne warms everyone, for a very long time, and whoever emits it pays nothing for that. To put a price on it, economists need to know how a tonne becomes warming, and what warming costs. The first half is physics, and it fits in four equations.

First, carbon. Each year's emissions are shared among four reservoirs in the atmosphere's exchange with the oceans and the land. Some of the extra carbon is taken up within years, some within centuries, and about a fifth stays for millennia. These fractions and timescales are the IPCC's. Second, the concentration: pre-industrial air held 278 parts per million, and every 2.1 billion tonnes of carbon left in the air adds one more. Third, forcing: the extra energy trapped, rising with the logarithm of the concentration, scaled up for the other greenhouse gases, and reduced by the sulphur pollution from coal, which reflects sunlight. Fourth, temperature: the surface warms until it sheds the extra energy, while the deep ocean slowly soaks up heat. How much warming a doubling of carbon dioxide finally brings, the equilibrium climate sensitivity, is set at three degrees, the IPCC's best estimate.

Does it work? The dots are the yearly concentration at Mauna Loa in Hawaii, where Charles Keeling began measuring in 1958: 427 parts per million in 2025. The line is the model, fed nothing but the emissions since 1750. Two numbers were fitted to the dots: how fast the reservoirs take up carbon, since the IPCC's response is for a single pulse added to today's air, and how much of the uncertain emissions from land use to count, 55 percent. The model misses the record by 0.8 parts per million on average.

And the temperature. In gold, the world's average surface temperature from HadCRUT5, measured from its level in 1850 to 1900. The wiggles are weather: El Niño years, volcanoes. In green, the model. Two more numbers were fitted here, with the sensitivity held at three degrees: how much the other greenhouse gases add to carbon dioxide's forcing, 36 percent, and how much the sulphur from burning coal cools, which is part of why the record flattened in the middle of the century. Over the last ten years the model is 1.30 degrees warmer than the pre-industrial level, and the thermometers 1.30. That is the physics of the next chapter's economy.
Dice: Chapter five. A climate-economy model, built.

In 1992 William Nordhaus joined an economy to a climate in a model he called DICE, the dynamic integrated climate-economy model. The version built here follows its latest form, DICE-2023, by Lint Barrage and Nordhaus, on the climate of chapter four. The economy is Part twenty's: capital, labour and saving, with world output of about 150 trillion dollars in 2025. Output brings emissions, at an intensity that falls about one and a half percent a year as economies grow cleaner on their own. Emissions warm the climate. And warming does damage: DICE-2023's estimate is 3.1 percent of world output at three degrees, rising with the square of the temperature. The damage feeds back into output. The world can cut emissions by a share mu, at a cost that rises steeply with the share, until cutting the last tonne costs the backstop price of 515 dollars in 2050. And a planner chooses how much to cut each year to make the sum of everyone's discounted well-being, now and in the future, as large as possible, raising the share it cuts by no more than three points a year, as old plants, buildings and cars are replaced.

Now run it. In red, business as usual: today's policies, which DICE-2023 reckons cut emissions about five percent, rising slowly. Emissions keep growing for decades, and by 2100 the world is 3.1 degrees warmer than before industry. In green, the path a planner would choose: cut 20 percent of emissions by 2030, 38 by 2050, 68 by 2100, and reach net zero around 2149. Warming peaks at 2.7 degrees, against the unchecked climb. That is the cost-benefit answer, with this model's damages and its modest discounting, and it misses the Paris Agreement's goal of well below two degrees. Whether it should is the subject of chapters six to eight.

How does a model built in a few hundred lines compare with Nordhaus's? Warming in 2100 under business as usual: 3.1 degrees here, 3.6 in DICE-2023, which counts from 1765 and has a hotter baseline. On the optimal path, 2.6 here and 2.6 there. The share of emissions cut by 2050: 38 percent here, 39 there. The carbon price that delivers it in 2050: 110 dollars a tonne here, 115 there. And the social cost of carbon, the damage a tonne emitted today does over its lifetime: 63 dollars here, 66 there; and at a discount rate of three percent, 88 against 87. The structure, not the details, does most of the work. Which means that the structure's choices, above all the discount rate, deserve the closest look.
PlayIt: Chapter six. Play it: choose the discount rate.

Here is what the model says one extra tonne of carbon dioxide, emitted in 2025, does. Its damage arrives as a stream, in lost consumption, year after year. About 1 dollar in 2030, 5 dollars in 2100, 13 in 2200. The stream grows, because much of the carbon stays in the air, the world stays warmer, and the economy it harms keeps growing. Added up without discounting, to the year 2300 alone, it comes to about 2,843 dollars. Nobody thinks the social cost of carbon is that. The question is how to compare a dollar in 2200 with a dollar today.

Your turn. Discounting at a rate r says a dollar in seventy-five years is worth one over one plus r, seventy-five times over. At one percent a year, a dollar of damage in 2100 is worth about 47 cents today; at two, 23; at three, 11; at five, under 3. Pause, and choose the rate you would use for damage that falls on people not yet born.

Here is what your choice implies. The social cost of carbon is the whole stream, discounted to today. At one percent, about 561 dollars a tonne; at two percent, 183; at three, 88; at five, 37. The gold squares are DICE-2023's own figures at the same rates, from 485 dollars at one percent to 32 at five. At three percent, 31 percent of the cost comes from damage after 2100. Nothing else in the model moves the answer this much. Halve the rate and the cost of a tonne roughly doubles or triples. So the next chapter asks where a discount rate should come from.
Ethics: Chapter seven. The social cost of carbon: ethics and evidence.

Frank Ramsey worked out in 1928 what the discount rate for consumption should be, if a society plans its saving well. The rate r is the sum of two terms. Rho, the rate of pure time preference: how much less a person's well-being counts simply because they live later. Eta, how fast an extra dollar matters less as people grow richer, times g, the growth of consumption per head, about 1.75 percent a year in the model. The second term is uncontroversial in kind: if our grandchildren will be richer, a dollar of damage to them costs them less than a dollar costs us now. The first term is the fight.

Two views of rho give two worlds. With a pure time preference of one and a half percent and an eta of 1.45, the discount rate is about 4 percent, close to what capital earns, a tonne costs 63 dollars, and the optimal path lets warming peak at 2.7 degrees. In 2006 the Stern Review, written for Britain's Treasury by Nicholas Stern, argued that it is unethical to count future people less merely for being later. It set rho at 0.1 percent, allowing only for the chance that humanity dies out, and eta at one. Then the discount rate is about 1.8 percent, a tonne costs 408 dollars in this model, emissions fall to zero by about 2060, and warming peaks at 1.9 degrees. The Review itself, with its own model, put the social cost at over three hundred dollars a tonne of carbon, over eighty a tonne of carbon dioxide. The model, the damages and the climate are the same. Only the weight on the future changed.

This is the clearest case in the course of a step from is to ought. What is: invested capital earns several percent a year; future people will probably be richer; a tonne does damage for centuries. What the step needs: a judgment about how much people not yet born should count against us, and whether the return on capital, which Nordhaus used to argue for a higher rate, is the right guide for choices that span generations. And what follows: the carbon price, and how much the world should cut now. Economists can make the consequences of each choice exact, as the model just did. They cannot make the choice for you.

And the numbers governments have used? Nordhaus's 2016 model gave 31 dollars a tonne, in 2010 dollars. The United States' interim interagency figure of 2021 was 51. DICE-2023, with damages nearly twice as large as its predecessor's, 66. This film's model, 63. In 2022 Kevin Rennert and colleagues, with newer evidence on damages and a near-term discount rate of two percent, found 185, with a range from 44 to 413. And the Environmental Protection Agency's 2023 estimate drew on that work: 190 dollars a tonne. Most of the gap between the low numbers and the high ones is the discount rate, as chapter six showed.
Tails: Everything so far used one number for the climate's sensitivity, three degrees. Nobody knows it exactly. Here are two beliefs about it, both centred on three degrees. In blue, thin tails: the chance of more than six degrees is 0.3 percent. In red, fat tails, as Martin Weitzman argued in 2009 the evidence allows: the same centre, but a 5.5 percent chance of more than six degrees. Weitzman's point was that the data cannot rule the fat tail out, because so few past climates resemble one forced this fast, and that the tail, not the centre, may drive what we should pay to avoid the risk.

Here is the problem with numbers. Let damages follow DICE below four degrees but steepen sharply above six, as many fear, and let a society that dislikes risk, with a relative risk aversion of two, ask what sure loss of consumption it would accept in place of the gamble. To compute it, someone must decide the worst warming the calculation allows. With thin tails the answer is about 5 percent whatever the cut-off: the extremes are too unlikely to matter. With fat tails it is 8 percent if nothing above six degrees is allowed, 38 at ten, and 96 at twenty: the answer is whatever the cut-off says. That is Weitzman's dismal theorem in miniature: with fat tails, expected damage can be dominated by catastrophes whose probability nobody can estimate. His conclusion was not that the number is infinite, but that climate policy is partly insurance, against outcomes too bad and too uncertain for a single best guess.

Climate scientists point to particular ways the tail could arrive. Tipping points: the loss of ice sheets, the drying of the Amazon, thawing permafrost releasing its methane, changes in ocean currents, each a change that feeds on itself once begun. Simon Dietz, James Rising, Thomas Stoerk and Gernot Wagner put eight of them into an integrated model in 2021. Together they raise the social cost of carbon by about 25 percent. And there is about a 10 percent chance they more than double it. The common thread: uncertainty about the climate is a reason to price carbon higher, not lower, because the outcomes we cannot rule out are worse than the ones we expect.
Instruments: Chapter nine. Taxes, permits and standards.

A carbon price can be set directly, as a tax, or indirectly, by capping emissions and letting firms trade permits. Part fifteen showed which is better when costs are uncertain. Carbon dioxide is a stock pollutant: one year's emissions add little to what is already in the air, so the damage of one more tonne hardly depends on how many are emitted this year. The damage line is nearly flat. Nobody knows in advance how cheap cutting will be. A tax set at the damage lets firms cut until their cost of cutting reaches it, the right amount whether cutting proves cheap or dear. A cap fixes the amount instead. If cutting turns out dear, it forces too much; if cheap, too little; the purple triangles are the waste. Martin Weitzman's rule from 1974: when damage is flat and costs uncertain, set the price. That favours a carbon tax, or a permit market with a floor and a ceiling on its price.

British Columbia ran the textbook experiment. In July 2008 the province taxed carbon at 10 Canadian dollars a tonne, rising five dollars a year to 30 in 2012. It was designed to be revenue neutral: every dollar raised was returned by cutting income taxes, so the tax changed what was cheap, not how much the government took. The rate was held for years, then rose again, to 40 dollars in 2019 and 80 in 2024, by then within Canada's national price. In March 2025 Canada's new prime minister ended the national consumer carbon price, and British Columbia abolished its own from the first of April. A tax that economists had held up for seventeen years lost the vote it needed. The economics of a carbon price is simple; its politics, as Part forty-seven showed, is not.

The European Union chose permits. A cap on the total emissions of its power plants and heavy industry, one permit for each tonne, auctioned or handed out, traded among the firms, so that those who can cut cheaply sell their spare permits to those who cannot, until every tonne carries the same price, and the cutting is done wherever it costs least. The market began in 2005. For years it issued too many permits, a recession cut emissions further, and the price stayed low, the cap's weakness that the last diagram warned of. Reforms withdrew surplus permits, and in February 2023 the price passed 100 euros a tonne for the first time.

Most climate policy is neither a tax nor a cap. A single carbon price makes every tonne cost the same, so cuts happen wherever they are cheapest. Standards, for the fuel economy of cars or the efficiency of appliances, are visible and popular, but each rule implies its own cost per tonne, and some are far dearer than others. Subsidies for clean power and electric cars are paid for by taxpayers, and partly reward what buyers would have done anyway. Why use them? Partly politics: subsidies are easier to pass than taxes, as British Columbia just showed. And partly because prices work badly in places: for technologies too new to be learned by anyone but the first buyer, the subject of chapter eleven, and for buyers who do not notice running costs, as Part forty-five's inattention suggests.
Clubs: Chapter ten. Leakage, borders and clubs.

Climate is a global public good, Part fifteen's problem on the scale of the planet. Every country gains from the others' cuts and pays alone for its own. Suppose one country prices carbon. Its steel and cement now cost more to make than its rivals'. Some production moves to countries without a price, and the emissions with it: leakage. The answer on offer is a border adjustment: charge imports for the carbon emitted in making them, as if they had been made at home. The European Union has built one. Importers began reporting the emissions in their goods in October 2023, and from January 2026 they pay for them, for cement, aluminium, fertilisers, iron and steel, hydrogen and electricity. A border adjustment protects a country's own carbon price. It also does something more: it gives other countries a reason to price carbon themselves.

William Nordhaus took the idea further: a climate club. Fifteen Island countries of different sizes. Cutting emissions costs each about one percent of its output; if the whole world cuts, each avoids damage worth about three percent. Everyone would gain if all cut. But each country gains only the part of the benefit its own cuts bring, which for any single country is too small. Start with everyone in the club, let countries leave whenever leaving pays, and with no penalty the club unravels to nobody. Now let members charge a uniform tariff on imports from non-members. Leaving now costs something. At 6 percent, 8 countries stay; at 9 percent, all 15. Nordhaus found the same in a far richer model: without sanctions on non-participants, the only stable coalitions are those that cut very little. The Kyoto Protocol had no such penalty: the United States never ratified it, and Canada withdrew. A club with a penalty can hold together.
Innovation: Chapter eleven. Learning curves and directed technical change.

The DICE model assumes the cost of clean energy falls at a slow, steady pace whatever anyone does. Here is what happened to one clean technology. The price of solar photovoltaic modules, after inflation: about 132 dollars a watt in 1975, 0.12 in 2025. A fall of 99.9 percent, more than three tenfold steps on this scale. Few forecasters expected it, and the question for climate policy is whether it was luck or something policy can cause.

In 1936 the aeronautical engineer Theodore Wright noticed that each doubling of the number of aircraft built cut the labour needed for one by a steady fraction. Plot the price of solar modules against the capacity installed worldwide, from 2000 to 2025, both on log scales. Capacity doubled about 11 times, and the points fall on a line: each doubling cut the price by about 30 percent. If cost falls because things are built, then building more now makes the technology cheaper for everyone later, a spillover the first buyers do not capture. That is an argument for subsidizing early deployment, on top of pricing carbon, that many economists accept, though how much of the fall came from learning, and how much from research and scale, is still argued.

Daron Acemoglu, Philippe Aghion, Leonardo Bursztyn and David Hemous asked a deeper question in 2012: what decides whether inventors work on clean or dirty technology? Here is a toy of their model on the Island, with clean and dirty inputs that substitute well. Left alone, inventors go where the market is biggest, and the dirty technology is ahead, so it keeps getting better and clean falls behind: path dependence. A modest carbon tax for forty years, the grey band, is not enough to turn it. The same tax with a subsidy for clean research makes clean research more profitable; once clean technology has caught up, inventors stay with it after the policy ends. A tax twice as heavy does it alone, at a higher cost to consumers. Their conclusion: with good substitutes, temporary policy can change the direction of technology for good, and acting early is cheaper than acting late.
Damages: DICE's damage function came from a synthesis of studies. Since 2012 economists have measured damage from the data directly. The idea: a country's weather varies from year to year, much as if by chance. Compare each country with itself, allowing for its own trends, and with every other country in the same year, to strip out world booms and busts. What is left is the effect of a hotter or cooler year. Melissa Dell, Benjamin Jones and Benjamin Olken found that a year one degree warmer cut growth in poor countries by about 1.3 percentage points, with no robust effect in rich ones. Marshall Burke, Solomon Hsiang and Edward Miguel found a single curve for all countries: output peaks where the average temperature is about 13 degrees and falls steeply in hotter places.

Here is that regression, run for this film on newer data. Temperatures for 185 countries from the ERA5 reanalysis, growth of GDP per head from the World Bank, 1961 to 2023, with Burke, Hsiang and Miguel's controls. The curve peaks near 10.5 degrees, a little cooler than their 13, and the marks along the bottom are the countries' own average temperatures. For a country averaging twenty-five degrees, a year one degree warmer means growth about 1.0 points lower; for a cool country, a little higher. Splitting the countries by income instead, as Dell, Jones and Olken did, gives -0.4 points for the poorer half, with a standard error of 0.3: the same sign as theirs, and much less certain. The open question is whether such losses add up, year after year, or fade as people adapt. If they add up, the damage from warming is several times DICE's.

Damage falls on people as well as output, and people adapt. Alan Barreca and colleagues found that the toll of very hot days in the United States fell by about 75 percent over the twentieth century, chiefly through air conditioning in homes. Days above ninety degrees Fahrenheit caused about 600 early deaths a year from 1960 to 2004, against some 3,600 had the old relationship held. And the fuels that warm the climate damage health directly. China gave free or cheap coal for winter heating north of the Huai River, and not south of it. Comparing people on either side, Avraham Ebenstein and colleagues found far dirtier air and life expectancy 3.1 years lower just to the north; each extra ten micrograms of fine particles costs 0.64 years of life. A tonne of carbon from coal comes with this local damage too, which is why cutting it can pay even before the climate is counted.
Power: Electricity is where much of the carbon is, and its markets have their own economics. The Island's power plants line up from cheapest to dearest to run, the merit order: hydro and nuclear, then coal, then two gas plants, then fast-starting peakers and oil. Demand for power at any moment barely responds to price, and the market price is set by the cost of the last plant needed to meet it. Every plant running is paid that price, so the cheap ones earn a margin that pays for building them. A carbon price shuffles this queue. At 50 dollars a tonne it adds about fifty dollars a megawatt-hour to coal, which emits about a tonne for each, twenty to gas, and nothing to hydro or nuclear. Coal moves behind both gas plants, and at the evening peak the price rises to 85 dollars: the tax changes which plants run, and every buyer pays it at the margin.

Over a day, demand on the Island swings from about twenty-two gigawatts at night to 35 at the evening peak. The price follows the merit order: coal sets it at night, the first gas plant by day, the second at the evening peak. Prices that vary through the day are what make batteries and flexible demand pay: buy power at night, sell or save it at the peak.

Now the danger. One Island firm, Dynamo, owns both gas plants, 14 gigawatts. If it offers all of its capacity at the evening peak, the price is 48 dollars, and Dynamo earns 21 thousand dollars an hour. If it declares just 2 gigawatts unavailable, the queue runs short of cheap plants, the peakers set the price at 95 dollars, and Dynamo earns 585 thousand an hour on what it still sells, nearly thirty times as much. Holding back 10 gigawatts drives the price to the market's cap of 250. When demand is near capacity, even a firm with a modest share can make a fortune by producing less, and it is hard to prove a plant was not really broken.

This happened. California opened its electricity market in 1998. From June to October of 1999, wholesale power cost 2.04 billion dollars; in the same months of 2000, 8.98 billion. Severin Borenstein, James Bushnell and Frank Wolak worked out what each plant would have offered in a competitive market. Of the increase, 21 percent was higher costs of production, as gas prices rose, 20 percent the rents any tight market pays, and 59 percent market power. Market power's share of all spending rose from 25 percent in 1998 to 50 in 2000. The lesson for climate policy: markets for power need watching, and the transition to clean electricity will run through markets like this one.
Practice: Chapter fifteen. In practice: energy, carbon and regulation.

Who uses environmental and energy economics? Traders of power, gas and carbon permits, in markets that price every hour, as in chapter thirteen. Regulators and market monitors, who watch for withholding and design the caps and the tariffs. Government agencies, which put a social cost of carbon into the cost-benefit analysis of rules on cars, power plants and buildings, and whose answers turn on the discount rate. Banks, insurers and central banks, assessing how climate change and climate policy could hit the value of assets and the loans against them. And fisheries managers and resource firms, setting quotas and royalties and deciding when to extract, Hotelling's question in practice.

Called it? A forecast about a resource running out. In March 1956 the geophysicist M. King Hubbert, then at Shell, fitted a bell-shaped curve to the oil found and produced in the United States and predicted that production would peak between 1965, his likeliest year, and 1970, then decline. The record, from the Energy Institute: production peaked in 1970 and fell for 38 years, to its low in 2008. For half a century Hubbert looked like a prophet. Then horizontal drilling and fracturing opened the shale, and in 2018 American crude output passed its 1970 peak; this series, which also counts natural gas liquids, passed it in 2015. The verdict: partly right. Right about the peak and the decline of the oil that could be got with the technology of his day; wrong that it was the end, for the reason Simon gave in the hook: prices high enough call forth new technology.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: how large the damage is, who can adapt, and the economics of the transition.

The first open question is the size of the damage. Chapter twelve measured what a country's own unusually hot year does: about a point of growth in hot, poor places. In 2024 Adrien Bilal and Diego Känzig measured something different: what happens when the whole world has a warm year. They found world GDP about twelve percent lower some six years after a global rise of one degree, about six times earlier estimates, because extreme weather strikes many places at once and trade carries the losses. Their social cost of carbon runs from about eight hundred to over thirteen hundred dollars a tonne in different versions of the paper, against 63 in this part's model and 190 in the American government's 2023 estimate. Others question whether global temperature can be separated from everything else that moves the world economy. If they are right, every number in this part's dials is too low.

The second is the transition itself. In the model, cutting emissions on the optimal path costs about 0.09 percent of world output in 2030 and 0.29 percent in 2050: small beside the economy, and smaller than the damage it avoids later. But averages hide who pays. Christophe McGlade and Paul Ekins estimated in 2015 that to hold warming to two degrees at least cost, more than eighty percent of the world's coal reserves, half its gas and a third of its oil would have to stay in the ground: assets on the books of firms and the budgets of governments that would be worth far less. Who bears those losses, how fast capital can move to clean energy, and what that does to interest rates and inflation, is the macroeconomics of the transition, and it is being written now.

The third is adaptation. It works: chapter twelve's air conditioners cut the toll of American heat by about 75 percent. But it costs money, and the hottest countries, where chapter twelve's curve falls fastest, are among the poorest, the least able to pay. And it is a set of choices: where people live, what farmers plant, what cities build, whether flood risk is priced into insurance and property. How much damage remains once people adapt, and who pays for the adapting, is the question on which the size of climate damage, and the fairness of climate policy, now turn.
